title: Coordinates, Lines & Graphs
coreInsight: An equation in two quantities describes coordinate pairs that satisfy a relationship, and slope measures a rate linking horizontal and vertical change.
targetLearnerRealization: Coordinates are ordered pairs satisfying relationships, and slope is a rate of vertical change per horizontal change.
learningObjectives: Read and plot ordered pairs with horizontal coordinate first.
Interpret a graph as the set of coordinate pairs satisfying a relationship.
Compute slope as vertical change divided by matching horizontal change.
Attach meaningful units to slope in context.
Distinguish a relationship's numerical slope from its apparent steepness under changing axis scales.

continuity.openingCallback: Turn a two-column table into ordered pairs without losing the axis labels or scale.
closingSeeds: Every point on a line satisfies the same two-variable relationship.
Slope is a signed rate with vertical units per horizontal unit.
Equations can test graph intersections exactly when a sketch is ambiguous.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Axis scale does not affect interpretation.
Slope is merely visual steepness independent of units.
A graph is a drawing rather than the set of solutions to a relationship.

beats.purpose: Turn labeled table rows into ordered pairs and surface coordinate order.
beats.expectedRealization: Each table row becomes (horizontal input, vertical output).
beats.transitionIn: A table already links two quantities. Plotting keeps the same pairings but gives each row a position.
beats.prompt: The table pairs time x with distance y. Which ordered pair represents the row x = 2, y = 5?

visual.ariaLabel: A table pairing x values zero through three with y values one, three, five, and seven

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The horizontal x-coordinate comes first: (2, 5).
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep the axis labels attached: x is horizontal and written first; y is vertical and written second.

visual.ariaLabel: Four plotted points from the table, including two comma five

steps.title: Preserve the row
steps.body: The row x = 2, y = 5 becomes (2, 5): move 2 horizontally, then 5 vertically.

resolution.takeaway: Coordinates are ordered: horizontal first, vertical second.

beats.purpose: Connect plotted points to an equation as a solution set.
beats.expectedRealization: A point belongs on a graph exactly when its coordinates make the relationship true.
beats.transitionIn: The four plotted points follow one rule: y = 2x + 1. Test a new pair without relying on the picture.
beats.prompt: Which point belongs on the graph of y = 2x + 1?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. At x = 4, the rule gives y = 2(4) + 1 = 9.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Substitute each first coordinate for x and compare the result with the second coordinate.

visual.ariaLabel: The line y equals two x plus one through five solution points

steps.title: Check the equality
steps.body: The pair (4, 9) makes 9 = 2(4) + 1 true, so it lies on the graph.

resolution.takeaway: A graph of an equation is the set of all coordinate pairs that satisfy it.

beats.purpose: Discover slope as a repeated rate between points rather than visual steepness.
beats.expectedRealization: Each horizontal increase of 1 produces a vertical increase of 2, so slope is 2 vertical units per horizontal unit.
beats.transitionIn: The equation test identifies points one at a time. Compare consecutive points to expose what stays constant along the line.
beats.prompt: From (1, 3) to (2, 5), x increases by 1. By how much does y increase?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The rise is 2 for a run of 1, and the same change repeats.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Subtract matching coordinates: vertical change 5 - 3 and horizontal change 2 - 1.

visual.ariaLabel: A line with a rise of two and run of one marked between two points

steps.title: Match the changes
steps.body: Moving from (1, 3) to (2, 5) changes y by 2 and x by 1.

steps.title: Form the rate
steps.body: Slope = vertical change ÷ horizontal change = 2 ÷ 1 = 2.

resolution.takeaway: Slope measures vertical change per horizontal change.

beats.purpose: Separate numerical slope from appearance under different axis scales.
beats.expectedRealization: Changing units per grid square can change apparent steepness without changing coordinate pairs or rate.
beats.transitionIn: A rise of 2 over a run of 1 defines the rate. Now stretch the paper without changing any coordinates.
beats.prompt: Two graphs plot the same coordinate pairs. One uses 1 unit per vertical square; the other uses 5 units per vertical square. Which claim is true?

options.text: The lines may look differently steep, but their numerical slope and relationship are unchanged.
The second line has five times the slope because each square is worth five units.
Changing scale makes the points stop lying on one line.
The coordinate order reverses when the vertical scale changes.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Scale changes the picture's proportions, not the coordinate changes themselves.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Slope uses coordinate units, not the raw number of grid squares. Preserve the same ordered pairs.

visual.ariaLabel: Two graph scale descriptions with the same coordinate relationship

steps.title: Read numbers, not angles
steps.body: The coordinate change remains 2 vertical units for each 1 horizontal unit. Only the screen distance used to display those units changes.

resolution.takeaway: Always read axis scales; visual steepness alone does not determine slope.

beats.purpose: Name coordinates, graph solution sets, and slope after the learner has used them.
beats.expectedRealization: A line unifies a solution set and a constant rate.
beats.name: Lines as solution sets; slope as rate
beats.conciseDefinition: An ordered pair (x, y) locates a point. The graph of an equation contains every pair that makes it true. On a nonvertical line, slope is the constant vertical change divided by the matching horizontal change.
beats.memoryHook: Horizontal first; test the pair; rise over the matching run.

beats.purpose: Attach contextual units to slope and verify the rate across separated point pairs.
beats.expectedRealization: Slope is 3 dollars per mile, while the 4-dollar value at zero miles is a separate starting amount.
beats.transitionIn: The line y = 2x + 1 rose 2 vertical units per horizontal unit. Give both axes real units and interpret the quotient.
beats.whyNow: The learner has formed slope geometrically and can now distinguish a rate from a starting value in context.
beats.entryBridge: Treat miles as horizontal input and dollars as vertical output.
beats.exitBridge: Both point pairs confirm the same 3 dollars per mile; the 4-dollar starting cost is not the slope.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A labeled coordinate graph with plotted data and a rise/run marker.
learnerPrompts: What are the vertical and horizontal changes between two delivery points, including units?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Cost increases by 3 dollars for each additional mile.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Divide the change in dollars by the matching change in miles; do not use the starting cost as the rate.

visual.ariaLabel: Delivery cost graph with slope three dollars per mile and starting cost four dollars

steps.title: Use matching changes
steps.body: From 0 to 2 miles, cost rises 10 - 4 = 6 dollars over 2 miles.

steps.title: Interpret the quotient
steps.body: 6 dollars ÷ 2 miles = 3 dollars per mile. The later points give the same rate.

resolution.takeaway: Slope carries vertical units per horizontal unit.

beats.purpose: Use line equations to decide exact geometric intersections that a sketch alone cannot settle.
beats.expectedRealization: A rectangle point on a line must satisfy both the line equation and the rectangle's coordinate bounds.
beats.transitionIn: A plotted line represents exact solutions, even when its drawing is tiny. Use equations to decide whether two lines truly reach a distant rectangle.
beats.whyNow: The learner understands ordered pairs, line equations, slope, and scale; this contest problem combines them in an exact intersection test.
beats.entryBridge: The rectangle covers 15 ≤ x ≤ 16 and 3 ≤ y ≤ 5. Derive each line's equation, then check its heights across that x-range.
beats.exitBridge: One exact corner survives both the line equation and rectangle bounds; visual closeness alone proves nothing.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The same coordinate grid, labeled axes, and change-based line equations used earlier.
learnerPrompts: What lines do the ordered pairs A, B, C, and D determine?
What coordinate ranges describe the rectangle?
Why does line AB touch exactly the corner (15, 5)?
Why does line CD remain below the rectangle across 15 ≤ x ≤ 16?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Only line AB's point (15, 5) lies on the rectangle, so the answer is 1.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Find each line's y-value at x = 15 and x = 16, then compare with the rectangle's vertical range 3 through 5.

steps.title: Write the lines
steps.body: AB has slope 1/3 through the origin, so y = x/3. CD has slope -1/2 and y-intercept 10, so y = -x/2 + 10.

steps.title: Describe the rectangle
steps.body: Its points satisfy 15 ≤ x ≤ 16 and 3 ≤ y ≤ 5.

steps.title: Test AB
steps.body: At x = 15, AB gives y = 5, the top-left corner. For larger x in the rectangle's width, AB is above y = 5, so it touches only that corner.

steps.title: Test CD
steps.body: CD gives y = 5/2 at x = 15 and y = 2 at x = 16, both below the rectangle. Only one point remains.

resolution.takeaway: A graph is an exact solution set; equations and coordinate bounds decide intersections that sketches cannot.

beats.whyNow: Return to the foundational location convention after the layered contest transfer.
beats.entryBridge: Read horizontal movement first and vertical movement second.
beats.exitBridge: The signs place the point in the correct quadrant.
learnerPrompts: Which signed movement supplies x, and which supplies y?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Four right and two down gives (4, -2).
beats.incorrectFeedback: Write the horizontal coordinate first: right is positive; down is negative.

steps.title: Order the movements
steps.body: Right 4 gives x = 4; down 2 gives y = -2. Thus P = (4, -2).

resolution.takeaway: Coordinates keep horizontal first, vertical second.

beats.whyNow: Use algebra rather than visual estimation to test a point.
beats.entryBridge: A point belongs exactly when its two coordinates make the equation true.
beats.exitBridge: Only one pair has zero equation error.
learnerPrompts: For each pair, does y equal 2x + 1?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Substitute the first coordinate for x and compare the result with the second coordinate.

steps.title: Test the pair
steps.body: At x = 3, the equation gives y = 2(3) + 1 = 7, matching (3, 7).

steps.title: Use the meaning
steps.body: Because the equality is true, the point lies on the graph.

resolution.takeaway: Graph membership is an equation check.

beats.purpose: Assess slope from contextual data with units.
beats.whyNow: Move from graph coordinates to a verbal two-point description.
beats.entryBridge: Pair the 10-kilometer change with the same 2-hour interval.
beats.exitBridge: The quotient is a rate in kilometers per hour.
learnerPrompts: What vertical and horizontal changes belong together?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. 10 kilometers over 2 hours is 5 kilometers per hour.

steps.title: Match changes
steps.body: Distance rises 10 kilometers while time rises 2 hours.

steps.title: Interpret slope
steps.body: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 kilometers per hour.

resolution.takeaway: Slope's units come from vertical units divided by horizontal units.

beats.purpose: Assess signed slope and consistent point order.
beats.whyNow: Change from increasing data to a line that falls as x increases.
beats.entryBridge: Use the same point order in both coordinate differences.
beats.exitBridge: The negative rate records a fall of 2 vertical units per unit right.
learnerPrompts: What signs do the y-change and x-change have when moving left point to right point?
beats.incorrectFeedback: From (-1, 5) to (3, -3), compute y-change -8 over x-change 4.

visual.ariaLabel: A decreasing line through negative one comma five and three comma negative three

resolution.takeaway: Negative slope means y decreases as x increases.

beats.purpose: Assess using a constant slope to extend a linear relationship.
beats.whyNow: Finish by carrying an established rise/run to a new point.
beats.entryBridge: Compare the two equal horizontal runs from 2 to 6 and from 6 to 10.
beats.exitBridge: Equal runs on one line produce equal rises.
learnerPrompts: How much does y rise when x increases by 4?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Another run of 4 adds another 10, giving y = 31.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The run from 2 to 6 is 4 and raises y by 10; repeat that change from x = 6 to x = 10.

steps.title: Find the repeated change
steps.body: From (2, 11) to (6, 21), a run of 4 produces a rise of 10.

steps.title: Extend the line
steps.body: From x = 6 to x = 10 is another run of 4, so y rises from 21 to 31.

resolution.takeaway: A line repeats the same vertical change for equal horizontal changes.

beats.purpose: Consolidate coordinate, scale, solution-set, and slope safeguards.
beats.expectedRealization: A reliable graph reading keeps order, scale, equation truth, and units connected.
beats.transitionIn: Tables, delivery costs, contest lines, locations, and travel rates all depended on the same checks.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable line-and-graph routine? Select all four.

options.text: Read axis labels, units, directions, and scale before interpreting shape.
Keep each point ordered as horizontal x first, vertical y second.
Use substitution to test whether a point satisfies the relationship.
Compute matching vertical change over horizontal change and attach units.

response.feedback: Each action protects a different meaning carried by the graph.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—read the axes, preserve order, test the equation, and interpret slope as a rate.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four matter; a sketch without its coordinates, scale, relationship, and units is incomplete.

visual.ariaLabel: Four safeguards for interpreting coordinate lines and graphs

steps.title: Use the graph as mathematics
steps.body: The picture organizes exact coordinate pairs. Its equation decides membership, and its slope quantifies change independently of display scale.

resolution.takeaway: Coordinates locate, equations verify, and slope measures change.

beats.purpose: Create an unresolved question about nonconstant rate without asserting a mapped successor.
beats.expectedRealization: A curve may have different rates of change in different intervals.
beats.transitionIn: A line repeated one rise for every equal run. Now imagine the plotted points bend away from any one line.
beats.prompt: If equal 1-hour intervals add 2 kilometers, then 5 kilometers, then 9 kilometers, what part of the slope routine must change when no single rate describes the whole graph?
beats.takeaway: Lines have one constant slope; changing relationships require comparing rates over chosen intervals.

notes: Design: a labeled table becomes plotted ordered pairs, which become the solution line y = 2x + 1. Repeated coordinate changes expose slope as rate before formal terminology. The closing asks how rate analysis changes when points no longer form a line.

Beat outline: table-to-points puzzle -> equation membership -> rise/run discovery -> scale trap -> name graph and slope -> generated delivery-rate anchor -> authentic line/rectangle transfer -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> curved-change hook.
A generic data-graph primitive was added for explicit axis scales, points, lines, and rise/run markers. It is static and inspectable; attempt visuals do not reveal response assignments.

The contest animation appears after submission with four prompts aligned to its four states. All generated answers were verified by coordinate calculations and independently by reconstruction, residual audits, or equal-run reasoning. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
